sections.b: Esther enters the story as Hadassah, an orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai in Susa (Esther 2:7). Taken with many other young women into the king's harem, she wins the favor and loyal love of the eunuch Hegai and then of the king, who makes her queen in Vashti's place (Esther 2:9, 17). Throughout, she does as Mordecai says and keeps her people secret (Esther 2:10, 20). The text uses passive verbs for her: she "was taken" and "was brought." Readers have judged this phase of her life very differently: as helpless obedience, as compromise with a gentile court, or as the ordinary survival of a diaspora Jew, in the manner of Joseph.

Chapter 4 is Esther's turning point. Told of Haman's decree, she first explains the law: anyone who goes to the king uncalled dies unless he holds out the gold scepter, and she has not been called for thirty days (Esther 4:11). Mordecai answers that the palace will not save her and that she may have come to royal power "for a time like this" (Esther 4:14). She then takes command: the Jews of Susa are to fast for her three days, she and her maids will fast too, and she will go in to the king against the law. "And if I perish, I perish" (Esther 4:16). From here on she gives the orders, and Mordecai obeys (Esther 4:17).

common: Esther is remembered as a model of courage, risking her life to save her people.
"For a time like this" is often quoted to mean that God places people where they are needed.
uncommon: Some readers, ancient and modern, see Esther as compromised by her marriage to a gentile king until Mordecai's challenge in chapter 4.
The Talmud says that Esther was passive in the king's bed and remained in her heart Mordecai's wife (Bavli Megillah 13b).

sections.b: Mordecai is introduced with a genealogy that points back to Saul: son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a man of Benjamin, from a family exiled with Jeconiah (Esther 2:5–6). He raises his orphaned cousin, tells her to hide her people, and walks past the harem court each day to learn how she is (Esther 2:7–11). Sitting in the king's gate, he uncovers a plot to kill the king, but his service is only written down, not rewarded (Esther 2:21–23). Then he refuses to bow to Haman, explaining only that he is a Jew (Esther 3:2–4), and so brings a death sentence on his people. In chapter 4 he mourns in sackcloth and sends Esther the charge that turns her into her people's champion (Esther 4:1–14).

common: Mordecai refused to bow to Haman because bowing to a man was idolatry.
uncommon: Some readers think the book leaves Mordecai's motive deliberately open, and some question whether his refusal was wise, since it endangered every Jew.

claude.title: Claude's theory: Mordecai's two kinds of openness
claude.body: My own observation: Mordecai is strangely double in chapters 2–4. He tells Esther to hide her people (2:10, 20), yet he tells the king's servants openly that he is a Jew (3:4). Read together, these suggest a man who judges each situation: secrecy where it protects the weak, openness where his own conscience is at stake. Chapter 4 brings the two together when he asks Esther to reveal what he had told her to hide. Commentators, among them Fox and Berlin, note the contrast; reading it as a deliberate study in when to hide and when to speak is my own suggestion.

sections.b: Haman appears without introduction except his name, his father's name and his label: "the Agagite" (Esther 3:1). Promoted for no stated reason, he expects everyone at the gate to bow. When Mordecai will not, Haman decides to destroy all the Jews of the empire (Esther 3:5–6). He casts Pur, the lot, to choose the day, tells the king of an unnamed people whose laws differ and who disobey the king, and offers 10,000 talents of silver (Esther 3:7–9). With the king's signet ring he sends out a decree in every script and language to kill every Jew on the thirteenth of Adar (Esther 3:10–13). The narrator now calls him "the enemy of the Jews" (Esther 3:10).

common: Haman is the classic villain of Jewish memory, and his name is drowned out with noise when the scroll is read at Purim.
uncommon: The Talmud identifies Haman with Memucan, the adviser who brought about Vashti's fall (Bavli Megillah 12b).

sections.h: The lot that named the feast (Esther 3)
sections.b: Purim takes its name from the lot Haman cast in the first month of Ahasuerus's twelfth year to choose the day of destruction: "Pur, that is, the lot" (Esther 3:7). The foreign word, Akkadian puru, is explained for Hebrew readers. The lot came out at Adar, the twelfth month, almost a year away, and the decree set the thirteenth of Adar for the killing (Esther 3:13). The days chosen for the Jews' destruction became the days of their rest and celebration (Esther 9:17–26). The book's many feasts, beginning with the king's in chapter 1, lead up to this one.

sections.h: Agag's heir and the son of Kish (Esther 1–3)
sections.b: Esther never names Amalek, but it sets up the old feud with care. Mordecai is "the son of Kish, a man of Benjamin" (Esther 2:5), from the family of Saul. Haman is "the Agagite" (Esther 3:1), recalling Agag king of Amalek, whom Saul spared against God's command (1 Samuel 15:8–9). Memucan's words about giving Vashti's place "to a neighbor of hers who is better than she" (Esther 1:19) echo Samuel's sentence on Saul for that failure (1 Samuel 15:28). Haman's decree to kill "little children and women" (Esther 3:13) mirrors the order Saul did not carry out (1 Samuel 15:3). Jewish tradition reads Esther as the next round of the war the LORD would wage "one generation after another" (Exodus 17:16), and the passage "Remember what Amalek did to you" (Deuteronomy 25:17) is read in synagogues on the Sabbath before Purim. Josephus calls Haman an Amalekite (Antiquities 11.209).

common: Haman was an Amalekite, a descendant of King Agag.
uncommon: Some scholars think "Agagite" is a literary label meant to recall Agag, not a claim about Haman's actual descent.

sections.b: Esther's first four chapters contain no miracle, no prophet and no prayer, and God is never named. Yet one event leads to the next: a king's drunken order and a queen's refusal empty the throne (Esther 1); a beauty search brings an orphan from a Jewish family to the palace, and she wins the favor of all who see her (Esther 2:8–17); a plot overheard in the gate is written in the records but not rewarded (Esther 2:21–23); a lot cast in Nisan puts the day of destruction eleven months away (Esther 3:7). In Esther 4:14 Mordecai draws the threads together: rescue will come "from somewhere else," and "who knows?" perhaps Esther became queen "for a time like this." The Talmud links Esther's name to God's hiding his face (Deuteronomy 31:18; Bavli Chullin 139b). Most Jewish and Christian readers take the book as the Bible's great picture of God working unseen; some critical scholars read it as a story of human courage that leaves the question open.

sections.b: With Daniel, Esther is one of only two books of the Bible set wholly among Jews in the east, and the only one set after the return, among Jews who stayed. Mordecai's family was exiled with Jeconiah (Esther 2:6, where the verb "exile" comes four times), and he and Esther live and work in the Persian capital. Haman describes the Jews as a people "scattered here and there, kept apart, among the peoples in every province" (Esther 3:8), words that recall Moses' warning: "The LORD will scatter you among the peoples" (Deuteronomy 4:27). When the decree comes, the Jews in every province mourn and fast together (Esther 4:3), a people dispersed but still one. The book addressed readers who lived in this condition and asked how to remain Jews in it.

Haman has pur, the lot, cast "day by day and month by month" to find the right day to destroy the Jews (Esther 3:7). The word is Akkadian, and an Assyrian clay die of the 800s BC calls itself a puru. In Israel lots were cast before the LORD, trusting him for the result (Leviticus 16:8; Joshua 18:6; Proverbs 16:33); Haman's lots are cast to find a lucky day. The lot gives the Jews eleven months, and in the end it names the feast that celebrates their rescue, Purim (Esther 9:24–26). Many readers see Proverbs 16:33 fulfilled: the lot is thrown, but the outcome is God's.

When the decree goes out, "the Jews mourned deeply. They fasted, wept and cried aloud" (Esther 4:3). Esther then calls a total fast, no food or water for three days, night and day, for the Jews of Susa, herself and her maids, before she risks her life (Esther 4:16). The Hebrew never says they prayed, although fasting in the Bible nearly always goes with prayer (Ezra 8:21; Nehemiah 1:4; Jonah 3:5–9). If the fast began after the decree of 13 Nisan, it fell over Passover, as the Talmud notes (Bavli Megillah 15a). Jews keep the Fast of Esther on 13 Adar, the day before Purim.

sections.h: The prayer that is not there (Esther 4)
sections.b: Esther is one of the very few books of the Hebrew Bible in which no one prays, and the only narrative book, and the absence is most striking in chapter 4, where the Jews fast, weep and wear sackcloth (Esther 4:1–3) and Esther calls a three-day fast before facing the king (Esther 4:16). Most readers assume prayer was part of it, as in every other biblical fast. The Greek Esther supplies it: after 4:17 it gives long prayers of Mordecai and Esther, in which they call on "the Lord, King over all" and explain their actions (Addition C). The difference between the two versions shows how much the Hebrew's silence was felt.

sections.h: A Jewish queen of a gentile king (Esther 2)
sections.b: Esther is married to a foreign king, a marriage Deuteronomy forbids for Israelites (Deuteronomy 7:3: "Do not marry into their families") and that Ezra and Nehemiah fought against in Judah in the same century (Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13:23–27). Esther does not choose it: she "was taken" (Esther 2:8, 16). The book does not comment, and readers have answered differently: some rabbinic readers excuse her as forced, the Greek Additions have her say she loathes "the bed of the uncircumcised" (Addition C), and many modern scholars see the book judging diaspora life by other standards than the Judean reformers. Like Joseph with his Egyptian wife (Genesis 41:45), she becomes the means by which her people are saved.

The Hebrew Esther never uses YHWH, Elohim, Adonai or any other name or title of God, although it mentions the king of Persia about 190 times. Some medieval readers found the divine name hidden in acrostics, the first or last letters of words in 1:20, 5:4, 5:13 and 7:7 spelling YHWH, and some Masoretic manuscripts write those letters large. Most scholars think these are chance or later devices. The Greek Esther names God more than fifty times. The rabbis' explanation, that God "hid his face" (Deuteronomy 31:18; Bavli Chullin 139b), made the absence itself part of the book's meaning.

Esther is the only book of the Hebrew Bible not found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and Purim does not appear in the Qumran calendars; whether this is chance or rejection is debated. The Talmud records an early rabbinic debate: the sage Samuel said Esther "does not make the hands impure." The Gemara explains that he held it was inspired to be read aloud but not to be written as Scripture; other sages, among them Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Akiva, argued that it was inspired outright (Bavli Megillah 7a). The rabbis nevertheless included it, and later tradition said it would outlast the Prophets. Among Christians, Melito of Sardis (about AD 170) left it off his list, Athanasius counted it outside the canon, and Luther wished it did not exist. The Greek Esther, with six Additions, is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians; Jerome moved the Additions to the end of his Latin version, and Protestants place them, if at all, among the Apocrypha.

Esther gives the Bible's fullest picture of the Persian court. Ahasuerus, almost certainly Xerxes I (486–465 BC), rules 127 provinces "from India all the way to Cush" (Esther 1:1) from the fortress at Susa. The book shows his banquets and display (Esther 1:3–8), the royal colors (Esther 1:6), the seven noble officials who see the king's face (Esther 1:14), the harem and its eunuchs (Esther 2:3, 14), the royal records (Esther 2:23), the signet ring and the scribes who write in every script and language (Esther 3:10–12), the royal post (Esther 3:13) and the deadly rules of access to the king (Esther 4:11). Many details match Greek and Persian sources; others, such as the irrevocable law (Esther 1:19) and the queens' names, have no outside support.

Mordecai is "the son of Kish, a man of Benjamin" (Esther 2:5), the father and tribe of Saul (1 Samuel 9:1), and his ancestor Shimei shares the name of the Benjaminite of Saul's clan who cursed David (2 Samuel 16:5). His enemy is Haman "the Agagite" (Esther 3:1), recalling the Amalekite king Saul spared (1 Samuel 15:8–9). Many Jewish and Christian readers see Esther as the story of a Benjaminite finishing what Saul left undone, and Memucan's phrase "a neighbor of hers who is better than she" (Esther 1:19) echoes Saul's sentence (1 Samuel 15:28).

sections.b: Esther echoes the Joseph story again and again. The officials' proposal to "name agents in each province" and gather the women (Esther 2:3) recalls Joseph's advice to Pharaoh (Genesis 41:34–35), and "The king liked the proposal" (Esther 2:4) recalls "Pharaoh liked the proposal" (Genesis 41:37). The servants speak to Mordecai "day after day," but he "would not listen to them" (Esther 3:4), as Joseph would not listen to Potiphar's wife (Genesis 39:10). The king slips off his signet ring for Haman (Esther 3:10) as Pharaoh did for Joseph (Genesis 41:42). Later come the royal robe and ride (Esther 6) and Mordecai's rise to second place (Esther 10:3). Most scholars think the writer of Esther used Joseph as a model for a Jew at a foreign court.

sections.h: A decree on the eve of Passover (Esther 3–4)
sections.b: Haman casts his lots in Nisan, the month of Passover (Esther 3:7), and the decree is written on the thirteenth of Nisan, the day before the feast (Esther 3:12). Esther's three-day fast (Esther 4:16) would then fall over Passover itself; the Talmud says Mordecai "passed over" the law by fasting on the feast (Bavli Megillah 15a, on Esther 4:17). Many readers see the timing as a deliberate echo: the old rescue from Egypt is remembered in the month a new threat begins, and the story ends with a new feast of rescue.

Esther 2 describes a royal harem in plain detail: young women gathered from every province, a year of beauty treatment, one night with the king, and then life as a concubine in "the second women's house" unless the king called for them again by name (Esther 2:12–14). Esther is one of these women until the king makes her queen (Esther 2:17). The narrator does not comment; modern readers often note the cost to the many women whose names the story never gives.

sections.h: Hanged on a pole in Persia (Esther 2:23)
sections.b: The two eunuchs who plotted against the king were "hanged on a pole" (Esther 2:23), the first of several such deaths in Esther (Esther 5:14; 7:10; 9:14). The Hebrew is the same "hang on a tree" of Deuteronomy 21:22–23 and Joshua 10:26. In Persia it probably meant impaling or displaying the body on a stake, as Herodotus says Darius did to three thousand Babylonians (Histories 3.159); the traditional English "gallows" suggests a rope and is misleading.

sections.h: Esther goes to the king for her people (Esther 4)
sections.b: Mordecai charges Esther "to plead for his grace and make her request to him for her people" (Esther 4:8). Her intercession is with an earthly king, not with God, and it puts her life at risk (Esther 4:11, 16). Christian readers have often seen in her a picture of intercession: one who stands between the people and the power that has condemned them, at her own cost, as Moses offered himself for Israel (Exodus 32:32). Jewish readers have seen in her and Mordecai the duty of those close to power to speak for their people.
